blocks.title: Dative bond
blocks.text: A dative bond is formed between two atoms when the shared pair of electrons is donated by one of the bonding atoms.

Consider the bond formation between H2O and a proton H+. Water has two covalent bonds and two lone pairs of electrons on the oxygen atom; the proton is deficient in electrons. The oxygen atom can therefore donate one lone pair to the acceptor H+, which results in a dative bond and the oxonium (hydronium) ion H3O+. Carbon monoxide also contains a dative bond between oxygen and carbon. Oxygen shares two valence electrons with carbon to make a normal double covalent bond, but the valency of carbon is not satisfied by these bonds; it needs one more pair to complete its octet, and oxygen donates one of its lone pairs to form a covalent bond that is a dative bond.

blocks.alt: Three examples of dative bonds. (a) A water molecule gives a lone pair on oxygen to H+, forming the hydronium ion H3O+. (b) Carbon monoxide: two shared pairs between C and O plus a dative pair from oxygen to carbon, drawn as an arrow from O to C. (c) Ozone: an O=O unit whose central oxygen (+) gives a lone pair to a third oxygen (-), drawn as an arrow. A note says both electrons of a dative bond come from one atom.
blocks.caption: Dative bond formation: (a) oxonium ion, (b) carbon monoxide, (c) ozone (original diagram after Figure 3.3).

blocks.text: Ozone is formed by a reaction between an oxygen molecule and an oxygen atom, a free radical. One of the oxygen atoms of the molecule donates a pair of electrons to make a coordinate covalent bond with this free radical, so the central atom has three bonds in all, a double covalent bond on one side and a coordinate covalent bond on the other. The central atom carries a positive charge, while the oxygen atom that accepts the lone pair carries a negative charge.
